title: Unsung women

segments.voice: Yesterday, failures too: the tradition naming its own worst days, and Adam and his wife saying we have wronged ourselves. Your line was honesty is faith. Did you say the plain sentence? Day one thousand fifty-three.

Mecca, a room within reach of the sanctuary. A woman sits with a book open in front of her. Across from her, men with pens and paper, scholars who traveled to be here. She reads Bukhari's collection of hadith aloud, line by line, and they copy it down, checking every word against what they hear, so that later they can say: I heard it from her. Her name is Karima al-Marwaziyya, and it went into the chain by which that book was passed on. Women were in this history the whole way through, often doing the work while someone else got the chapter. Today: unsung women.
screen: `A WOMAN READS; SCHOLARS WRITE.` → `I HEARD IT FROM HER.` → `THE WORK, WITHOUT THE CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an sets the frame. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! I suffer not the work of any worker, male or female, to be lost." The chronicles might drop a name; the verse says the work isn't dropped. So let's pick some back up, four kinds, all names this path has already met. First, a founder. In Fez, tradition says a woman named Fatima al-Fihri used her inheritance to found the mosque that became al-Qarawiyyin, a place of study. Second, a teacher: Karima, in that room in Mecca, a woman whose reading of Bukhari's collection men traveled to hear. Third, a poet. In Sokoto, Nana Asma'u wrote poems in several languages to teach the faith, and trained women teachers who carried those lessons to women in villages far from her. Fourth, a patron. Zubayda, wife of the caliph Harun al-Rashid, whose name tradition gives to the wells and stations of the pilgrim road from Iraq to Mecca, and other women after her who paid for schools, fountains and mosques with their own wealth, their names cut into a stone over a door that passersby rarely stop to read. Founders, teachers, poets, patrons. What ties them together is that the history needed them and often forgot to say so. The lesson for an ordinary day isn't only about the past. Look around any mosque, school or family today and ask who is doing work that nobody writes down.
screen: `NO WORKER'S WORK IS LOST, MALE OR FEMALE.` · `A FOUNDER: FATIMA AL-FIHRI IN FEZ.` · `A TEACHER AND A POET: KARIMA, NANA ASMA'U.` · `A PATRON: ZUBAYDA'S WELLS.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one woman's name. Settle, and breathe. Start with the names from today: Zubayda, Fatima, Karima, Asma'u. Say them slowly, one per breath. Then think closer to home. Who is the woman in your own story whose work made something possible and never got the credit? A mother who kept the house running, a teacher, an aunt who taught the prayers, a colleague who did the unseen part of a project. Say her name too, quietly, if you know it. If you don't, decide to find it out. The bell holds the time.
Unsung women. The founders, teachers, poets and patrons whose work built Muslim history, often without the credit. Today's word.
Your line: they were there. Today, learn the name of one woman behind something you use, a school, a mosque, a recipe, a road, and say it out loud once. Day one thousand fifty-three.

howItsDone: Muslim communities remember women such as Khadijah, Aisha and Fatimah from the Prophet's household, and local histories honor women who founded mosques, schools and charitable endowments.

Zubayda, Fatima al-Fihri, Karima al-Marwaziyya and Nana Asma'u were each taught earlier this year (days 914/1045, 916/919, 1032, 975); this day gathers them as a reflection and repeats only claims made there. Fatima's founding is framed as 'tradition says'.
'Nana Asma'u wrote poems in several languages' follows day 975 (Arabic, Fulfulde, Hausa).
'Other women after her who paid for schools, fountains and mosques' is a general statement about endowments (waqf), with no names or counts.
Editor: hook fixed a contradiction (the road bears her name, yet pilgrims 'drank without knowing who paid'); Zubayda's wells now framed as 'tradition says'.

Audit: the hook opened on Zubayda's wells on the pilgrim road, the same image day 1045 (Hajj caravans) used eight days earlier and 1046's review repeated. The hook now opens on Karima al-Marwaziyya reading Bukhari's collection in Mecca; Zubayda stays as the patron in the teach's fourth turn. Detail 'checking every word against what they hear' describes the general practice of sama' (audition); Keeper to confirm.
